| `PCR-seq-primers-v1-public` | 40/40 | 100.0% |
| `Prop-seq-gcpercent-v1-public` | 34/40 | 85.0% |
| `RE-seq-lenfrags-v1-public` | 32/40 | 80.0% |
| `RE-seq-numfrags-v1-public` | 28/40 | 70.0% |

`RE-seq-lenfrags-v1-public` includes the correct diagnostic retry; the original result was 31/39. `PCR-gene-gibshindprimers-v1-public` includes one output-budget exhaustion, scored incorrect. ProtocolQA and CloningScenarios each have one public subtask label, so their subtask scores equal their component scores above.

</details>

The original run took **1h13m50s including setup**, at concurrency 8. Reported inference cost was **$1.6401**, plus **$0.0041** for the two diagnostic retries (about **$1.65 total**). This excludes Iris CPU costs and any unreported charges for the two original failed responses. Runtime is specific to this model, route and concurrency; policy adoption still needs a runtime-budget discussion, including representative subsetting if necessary.

Settings: standard requests (not batch), high reasoning, 128000-token output ceiling, seed 42, 1200-second per-request timeout, and no automatic retries. Temperature/top_p were omitted because the route does not advertise support. The two diagnostic requests used concurrency 1 and unchanged request bodies. Both completed normally; the original JSON failures were not reproduced and their cause remains unknown. Raw HTTP capture has since been fixed and checked offline, without new model calls.

This uses `marin-labbench-no-tools-v3`: no tools, no added abstention option, generated reasoning allowed, final `Answer: X`, and the shared letter-choice grader. These are scores for the Marin forced-choice variant, not a reproduction of the authors' uncertainty-calibration protocol. Dataset answers and scientific conventions were left unchanged.

Execution used a private Iris launcher making direct OpenRouter requests with Evalchemy's prompt builder and grader. It does **not** establish native Marin launcher → EvalDash validation. PR #10582 remains draft.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 Compared **1,967 public LAB-Bench v1 rows with 1,912 LABBench2 rows**, including v2 sequence attachments and protocol PDFs, to assess overlap relevant to using v1 as ID and v2 as a held-out evaluation.

**The overlap varies by category.** LitQA contains confirmed reused questions. SeqQA and ProtocolQA retain substantial skill overlap, even when the inputs or answers change. CloningQA shifts toward complete protocol design. Shared papers or vector sequences alone do not establish duplicate questions.

The tables combine automated measurements with direct inspection of questions and reference answers. Short quotations come from the [LABBench2 paper, §2](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2); the semantic assessments are ours. Counts are identified overlaps, not exhaustive semantic-duplication rates.

| V1 → V2 category | Paper’s description | Measured overlap and semantic assessment |
|---|---|---|
| LitQA2 → **LitQA3** | “ported from LitQA2”: some adapted questions; most are new. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **≥43/168 (25.6%) confirmed carryovers:** 19 identical and 24 reworded questions. Other inspected questions seek new facts using the same literature-retrieval skills. |
| FigQA → **FigQA2** | “all new questions”, with image, PDF and retrieval variants. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **30/101 (29.7%)** retrieval rows share papers with v1. Inspected pairs generally ask for different measurements using familiar figure-reading skills. **One strong same-fact candidate**, pending image-context verification. |
| TableQA → **TableQA2** | New questions and the same three input variants described above. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **86/100 (86%)** retrieval rows share papers with v1. Strong continuity in table-reading skills, often with a different target cell or comparison. **One strong same-fact candidate**, pending image-context verification. |
| SuppQA → **SuppQA2** | “carried forward”: supplementary-material retrieval in open-response form. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **1/125** shares a source and ID but asks a different question. Same skill—retrieving primers, parameters and other experimental details—with generally different targets in the inspected sample. |
| DbQA → **DbQA2** | Broader and more specific database coverage (paraphrased). [§2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS2) | No exact-question, ID or source-identifier matches across **86 rows**. Broader tasks across **43 named sources**, but continuing database skills; ClinVar and Ensembl appear in both. No obvious same-fact reuse in the inspected comparisons. |
| SeqQA → **SeqQA2** | “a similar approach”: 20 templates × 20 instances, including new subcategories and file/retrieval inputs. [§2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS3) | **40/400 (10%)** share DNA segments ≥100 bases with v1: all Gibson-primer and restriction-cloning primer-design rows. **Substantial skill overlap** in GC content, restriction analysis, ORFs and primers, alongside new operations and sequence-design tasks. These are not 40 confirmed duplicates. |
| ProtocolQA → **ProtocolQA2** | “extends the same approach”: error-injected protocols, with more complex protocols and PDF inputs. [§2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS4) | **8/125 (6.4%)** reuse underlying protocols from two v1 questions: seven western-blot variants and one plasmid-preparation variant. Different injected errors and answers, but **the same troubleshooting task family**. |
| CloningScenarios → **CloningQA** | No explicit description of overlap. [§2.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS5) | **14/14** share DNA segments ≥100 bases with v1. However, inspection of all 33 v1 and 14 v2 prompts found no obvious identical full scenario. **Substantial planning/output shift:** answer questions about a scenario → construct a complete protocol and reagent designs. |

**New categories:** the paper introduces **PatentQA (121 rows)**, **TrialQA (120 rows)** and **SourceQuality / SourceQualQA (150 rows)** as “new subtask types” ([§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1)), with no direct v1 category counterpart. No exact-question, ID or normalized source-identifier matches were found for these categories; semantic examples are included below.

<details>
<summary>Concrete examples behind the semantic assessments</summary>

- **LitQA:** a carryover asks the same relationship between intron and exon methylation, with minor wording changes. Other inspected v2 questions ask for unrelated experimental doses or protein-interaction details.
- **FigQA:** on a shared neuroscience paper, v1 asks which stimulus maximizes a population-distance change; v2 asks what percentage of virgin males responds to social cues. These are different measurements. In the stronger reuse candidate, both versions ask which gene is enriched in both donors during the expansion screen; both answer CRKL. Candidate pair: v1 `69112914-26ca-4430-bd2a-6720d0e03b05` → v2 `dad00259-ca31-41a7-aeba-f8e6e577b1d8`.
- **TableQA:** on the same profilin study, v1 asks which mutation most affects pI; v2 asks the pI of the H120E mutant. In the stronger reuse candidate, both ask for the number of protein-interaction databases in the same review and answer seven. Candidate pair: v1 `6036c219-fd8c-408b-b0e5-a2eaaecbc596` → v2 `a102bad7-90a7-4cc9-a8b9-82665bdc96ca`. Neither figure/table candidate has been confirmed against the original images.
- **SuppQA:** the shared Gene-SGAN row changes from a hyperparameter value to which network component has a bias term. Other examples retrieve primer sequences for different genes or constructs.
- **DbQA:** v1 asks which gene occupies a chromosome band; v2 asks for sequence around a specified gene's transcription start site. V2 also includes expression aggregation, coordinate conversion and structure counts. Shared database names can appear in prompts even when source metadata does not match.
- **SeqQA:** the inspected Gibson pair retains pUC19/SmaI but changes the gene and organism: v1 selects primers, v2 produces them. In one inspected v2 attachment pair, the DNA match came from pUC19, not the supplied genome. New v2 operations include alignment entropy, molecular weight and enzyme kinetics.
- **ProtocolQA:** the shared western-blot protocol tests excess BSA in v1; v2 variants test incubation time, transfer, blocking or detection chemistry. Same experimental workflow, different faults to diagnose.
- **CloningQA:** v1 usually asks about a component or outcome of a supplied scenario, including some protocol-selection questions. V2 asks for complete protocols using Gibson, restriction/ligation or Golden Gate. Familiar techniques transfer, but the required solution is more extensive.
- **PatentQA / TrialQA:** examples ask for patent sequence identifiers and parameter ratios, or trial eligibility thresholds and differences between treatment-arm restrictions. No same-fact v1 counterpart appeared in the inspected candidates.
- **SourceQuality:** reference reasons include nonrandomized study design, the wrong intervention comparison or a missing outcome. We inspected the questions and reference reasons, rather than independently reassessing each paper's scientific eligibility.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Audit scope, inspection coverage and limitations</summary>

**Data:** pinned [v1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench/tree/5c77cec648430f30611808808861eb86f81d5eaa) and [v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/EdisonScientific/labbench2/tree/3678e7e38748477d0606407468db9cd7e2f2e667) revisions. Counts refer to these public revisions and differ from some paper counts. V2 totals include separate figure/table input variants, not 1,912 distinct underlying questions. V1's private holdout was unavailable.

**Automated checks:** IDs, exact and normalized questions, source identifiers, similarity-based candidates, protocol text and exact DNA segments. No identical question strings were found outside LitQA. Figure/table source-overlap counts in the main table use retrieval variants; image and PDF variants each had 30/101 matches for FigQA and 82/100 for TableQA.

**Direct semantic inspection:** all 86 DbQA2 prompts; all 33 v1 and 14 v2 cloning prompts; one example per SeqQA2 template (20), v1 SeqQA template (15) and v1 DbQA template (10); and six deterministically selected rows each from LitQA3, FigQA2, TableQA2, SuppQA2, ProtocolQA2 and the three new categories, alongside candidate v1 matches. We also revisited the identified protocol pairs and figure/table candidates, supplementing the earlier review of the 43 LitQA carryovers. DbQA inspection was not an exhaustive comparison against all 520 v1 rows.

**Limits:** semantic findings describe inspected examples and task families, not a measured percentage of semantic duplicates. Figure/table inspection used retrieval questions and reference answers, without verifying the original images. Source matching does not resolve alternate URLs or missing metadata. DNA checks covered contiguous A/C/G/T strings in v1 question text and supplied v2 sequence files, including reverse complements; they excluded answer/distractor-only sequences, runtime-retrieved inputs and approximate similarity. One v2 protocol PDF yielded no extractable text. The paper gives no category-by-category numerical overlap audit; our measured overlaps should not be attributed to the authors.

</details>

issues.title: [eval] Add no-tools LAB-Bench evaluations with separate component scores

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
Add the original 5,200-question [GenomeQA benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05774) to Evalchemy: one generated answer per question, no tools or retrieval, exact option-letter accuracy, and primary reporting by biological subtask alongside the overall score. Binary-choice (BCQ) and multiple-choice (MCQ) summaries remain available for diagnostics and paper comparisons. Preserve all 12 task-by-format accuracies and their denominators. This measures raw DNA sequence understanding across six task families.

The decisions below define the proposed implementation. Admission into Marin’s official evaluation policy remains separate. Implementation assumptions were audited against Marin main `fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3`. Source inspection and a data-equivalence check are complete; implementation is in progress on `codex/genomeqa`, and no model evaluation has been launched.

Decisions and alternatives considered:

| Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale and tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use pinned HF `binary` and `mcq` data. | Load the authors’ twelve JSONL files directly; rebuild questions from upstream biological databases. | All 5,200 HF rows matched the author release on evaluation fields. HF fits existing loading components. Direct JSONL would also be valid but offers little functional benefit after the equivalence check. Rebuilding could change sampling, filtering, and questions. Metadata equivalence remains unchecked. |
| Evaluate the original full benchmark. | Carbon’s modified MCQ dataset; 600-row or organism-specific subsets. | Preserve the original six task families and both formats. Carbon changes the taxonomy task; subsets change coverage. Neither should silently replace the original benchmark. |
| Use Evalchemy’s existing execution components. | Adopt the authors’ runner or Carbon’s Inspect evaluator as the execution path. | The task is direct generated-answer Q&A and fits the existing Evalchemy runtime. Reuse loading, requests, response handling, storage, and resume; preserve the selected benchmark protocol independently of its original runner. |
| Report raw accuracy. | Normalize accuracy relative to chance. | Ordinary correct/total accuracy is interpretable and preserves the paper’s metric. BCQ and MCQ have different chance levels; retain their separate results rather than changing the metric to compensate. |
| Weight the six subtasks equally and the two formats equally. | Pool all 5,200 questions into micro-accuracy. | Pooling would give motifs five times less weight than each other family because it has fewer questions. Equal weighting treats each biological capability as one component. |
| Foreground six subtask scores and their overall mean. | Foreground BCQ/MCQ summaries; show only a combined score; show only the two format scores. | The research priority is understanding biological strengths and weaknesses. First average BCQ/MCQ within each subtask, then average subtasks. Reversing that order gives the same overall number with equal weights; the decision concerns presentation. Keep all 12 cells and both format summaries as secondary diagnostics. |
| Retain the authors’ fixed optimized system prompt and user layout. | Minimal generic prompting; Carbon’s Inspect multiple-choice prompt; repeat prompt optimization. | Use an established prompt for the original questions and avoid introducing an additional variable. Optimization already occurred offline; the fixed prompt is in the public runner. The resulting scores measure capability with supplied biological guidance. Generic prompting could support a separate ablation, but is not part of this integration. |
| Reuse shared extraction with final-section isolation and valid-option checking. | Copy the authors’ complete parser; use the shared HLE/GPQA extractors unchanged; introduce a separate extraction implementation. | Synthetic checks showed that shared extractors can select incidental analysis or trailing letters. A small preprocessing step preserves reuse while identifying the intended final answer. This deliberately adapts the author parser rather than claiming exact extraction parity. |
| Accept an unambiguous explicit `Answer: X` when the heading is missing. | Require the exact `### Answer` heading for every response. | A clearly stated answer should not be marked wrong solely for omitting a heading. Conflicting markers and missing answers still require focused validation; do not recover answers from hidden reasoning. |
| Apply one shared total generated-token cap across models. | Model-specific recommended caps; leave limits to provider defaults as the author runner does; cap only the answer text. | Bound generation consistently across a large question set. Include reasoning, visible analysis, and final answer. This equalizes nominal token allowance, not compute, latency, or tokenizer efficiency. Provider semantics must be verified. |
| Start with 16,384 generated tokens per question. | Start with 32,768 tokens. | Limit cost and latency over 5,200 questions. The tighter cap may increase truncations; report them by model and subtask. This is an initial evaluation choice, not a budget validated by the GenomeQA paper. |
| Enable thinking where supported and pin effort per model configuration. | Always use provider-recommended mode, including thinking off; use the same named effort for every model; use maximum effort everywhere. | Follow the GPQA/MMLU-Pro thinking-on pattern in the current policy. Identical effort labels do not imply equivalent reasoning across providers, and maximum effort may exhaust the total budget before an answer. Concrete effort values remain to be specified per model. |
| Request temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95. | Provider-recommended sampling; temperature 0 as in MMLU-Pro; Carbon-X’s 0.6/0.95/top-k 20 settings. | Retain the settings requested by the released GenomeQA runner alongside its prompt. Marin’s reasoning-Q&A precedents are mixed: GPQA uses 0.7, MMLU-Pro uses greedy generation. This is a GenomeQA protocol choice, not a universal Marin rule. Document unsupported provider parameters and deviations. |
| First-pass paper comparison: Llama-4 Maverick on the complete TF-motif MCQ cell (100 questions). | No paper-model check; a full 5,200-question run; a 600-question stratified sample across all 12 cells; the complete enhancer/promoter MCQ cell (500 questions). | A complete cell permits direct comparison with an entry in the paper’s table; a cross-cell sample would use different question coverage. Motif MCQ is the smallest complete cell, and Maverick avoids reasoning-effort ambiguity. Limit the comparison to this complete cell; a full-benchmark parity run remains out of scope. |
| Proceed with independently written integration code and runtime HF loading; do not redistribute benchmark questions. | Wait indefinitely for author permission; vendor the upstream code, prompt, and dataset together. | An author response is not a prerequisite for adapter development. Keep the dataset license explicitly unspecified, use synthetic test fixtures, and keep question text out of public artifacts. Runtime fetching reduces redistribution but does not resolve missing dataset-use terms. |
| Keep the pinned runner prompt external and load its string without executing upstream code. | Bundle the runner prompt; use the CC BY paper’s Figure 8 prompt; write a new prompt. | Figure 8 is shorter than the runner: it omits the explicit binary-letter instruction and some reasoning guidance. Using it would change the agreed protocol. External loading preserves that protocol without bundling the prompt; it does not establish a license for the external asset. |

Open implementation details:

- Map the shared total cap to each selected provider. Prefer a native combined cap. If only independent hard caps exist, choose and record allocations summing to 16,384; this allocation has not been decided. Flag routes without equivalent enforcement rather than claiming equal limits.
- Pin concrete reasoning effort and any necessary sampling exceptions per model, and verify the effective request. Agreement on the policy does not establish endpoint-specific behavior.
- Validate conflicting/malformed answer handling, macro aggregation with missing cells, and how primary subtask scores appear in the dashboard.
- The agreed first-pass target is the complete 100-question motif MCQ cell on Maverick. Before execution, pin the provider and effective configuration and state the cost and duration bounds. This draft does not itself launch a run or authorize additional evaluations.

Data and provenance:

- Load `HuggingFaceBio/genomeqa` at revision `e655e415fa30681dddbaf4acc182bcbd8ac41943`, using only `binary/train-00000-of-00001.parquet` and `mcq/train-00000-of-00001.parquet`. Both use a split named `train`; these are the benchmark evaluation questions, not permission to train on them.
- Treat the [authors' release](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/tree/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d) as the protocol reference. Use the released questions rather than reconstructing samples from ENCODE, JASPAR, RefSeq, or other upstream biological databases.
- A full row comparison on 2026-11-05 found zero mismatches in question text, ordered options, correct answer index, or correct answer text across all 5,200 rows. Matching used `(format, subtask, id)`; each format had 2,600 unique keys, with no missing or extra rows. Metadata equivalence was not checked. Each format has 500 rows in each of the first five families and 100 motif rows.
- Binary Parquet SHA-256: `0ef4c3d33541980e3fded9a5b23a952296ce3c51cb0415b42c0299a61c21938a`. MCQ: `c1cbb51449eb8a5241890337c88dc1bc0a58974b8eb4cb8bc49f310b12faeb75`.
- Preserve option order and DNA text exactly. Use composite IDs; integer IDs alone repeat across subtasks. Do not expose answer or metadata fields to the model.
- Exclude `*_600`, organism subsets, `eukaryote_cls`, and `mcq_carbon*`. The [dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceBio/genomeqa/blob/e655e415fa30681dddbaf4acc182bcbd8ac41943/README.md) distinguishes these derivatives. In particular, Carbon replaces the broad taxonomy questions with within-eukaryote classification.

Scoring:

For a complete evaluation, let `a[s,f] = correct[s,f] / questions[s,f]` for family `s` and format `f`. The pinned denominator is 500 per cell, except motif cells, whose denominator is 100.

```text
Subtask score[s] = (a[s,BCQ] + a[s,MCQ]) / 2
GenomeQA macro = sum(Subtask score[s] for the six families) / 6

Secondary summaries:
BCQ macro = sum(a[s,BCQ] for the six families) / 6
MCQ macro = sum(a[s,MCQ] for the six families) / 6
```

Foreground enhancer/promoter identification, splice-site identification, taxonomy, histone marks, TFBS, and motifs. The overall score also equals `(BCQ macro + MCQ macro) / 2`; the order of averaging does not change equal weighting. Do not silently average available cells when a component is missing.

The format-level macro averages match the authors' [aggregation code](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/blob/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d/collect_res.py). The combined score is our explicitly defined summary over the 12 cells; do not call it a separately published paper headline. A pooled accuracy over all questions would underweight motifs by a factor of five relative to each other family. Do not average internal labels/question dimensions as additional equal-weight tasks. Retain their diagnostic breakdowns where useful.

Report raw accuracy, without chance correction; chance is 50% for BCQ, 25% for MCQ, and 37.5% for the combined summary. Model refusals, missing or unparseable final answers, and output-limit truncations score zero and stay in the denominator. A truncation scores zero even if a candidate answer appears before the cutoff. Preserve distinct refusal, parse-failure, and truncation diagnostics rather than classifying all failures as parsing errors.

The current runtime has a separate task-level guard: [`completion_response_text_unavailable()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/vendor/evalchemy/eval/robust_api.py#L52-L55) triggers when at least half of responses are classified empty, and the execution driver then skips aggregation. Resolve this interaction explicitly for GenomeQA: preserve zero grades and diagnostic counts for completed empty model responses, including an all-empty fixture, while retaining the guard's diagnostic evidence. Do not silently relax other benchmarks' failure behavior. A grader-only change is insufficient to meet this requirement.

Transport failures and missing results remain ungraded infrastructure failures, not incorrect model answers. A complete score requires all expected questions to have a grade. For incomplete runs, retain cell-level diagnostic `correct / graded` alongside expected, graded, and infrastructure-missing counts, labeled partial; do not substitute this denominator into a full-benchmark score or silently drop a missing cell. Do not emit a complete overall score while any cell is incomplete. If future official policy adoption permits publication with infrastructure failures, define its denominator and eligibility rules explicitly at that time; this integration does not establish a new release-policy exception.

Prompt and parser:

Use the fixed optimized system prompt and user-message layout in the authors' [run.py](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/blob/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d/run.py), preserving the `Question`, `Options`, and final instruction formatting. No new prompt search is needed. Prompt optimization was an offline pilot followed by manual refinement; the resulting prompt is actually embedded in the public runner, despite its variable name `SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT`. Freeze and identify that prompt in result provenance. Development-set disjointness from the full release has not been established here.

Agreed extraction approach: reuse the shared multiple-choice extractor with a small GenomeQA-specific preprocessing step. Prefer provider final-response content and isolate the last `### Answer` section when present. If that heading is absent, accept an unambiguous explicit `Answer: X` in the final-response content. Restrict extracted letters to the current question’s options. Do not use an LLM judge or search hidden reasoning for a missing final answer. Conflicting explicit answer letters in the selected final section are unparseable; without the heading, conflicting explicit letters are also unparseable. Do not apply an unrestricted last-letter fallback to the full response. Keep these rules explicit and test incidental option letters so the shared fallback cannot silently choose from analysis. This is a documented adaptation rather than exact reproduction of the authors’ parser.

Implement selection at the response/grader boundary, before conversion to a plain string. Reuse the vendored runtime's response handling and shared extraction with a thin benchmark-scoped wrapper that does not change other benchmarks' grading semantics. Preserve the raw response, selected parsing span, extracted letter, and failure reason in per-item artifacts. At the audited revision, [`letter_choice`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/vendor/evalchemy/eval/graders/math_specs.py#L63-L70) still stringifies the response before shared extraction. Reuse `CompletionText.response`, `CompletionContentPolicy.FINAL_ONLY`, and [`final_response_text()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/vendor/evalchemy/eval/graders/answer_extraction.py#L40-L47) for final-channel selection and supported thinking-marker cleanup, then apply the GenomeQA section and option rules. The shared boxed-answer helper can fall back to reasoning-only content and is unsuitable unchanged for this protocol. Check `finish_reason` before extraction so every output-limit truncation scores zero.

Sampling, reasoning, and token limits:

- Agreed sampling configuration: request temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95, matching the authors’ released runner. Verify that each provider accepts these parameters; document any required omission or deviation rather than silently substituting defaults. The released code establishes requested settings, not proof that every provider honored them in historical paper runs. Enable thinking where supported, following the GPQA/MMLU-Pro pattern in policy #10197. Resolve and pin actual reasoning effort in each model configuration; do not impose a universal effort label. Models without a thinking mode use ordinary generation. All models retain the shared 16,384-token total generation cap. Provider-specific parameter mappings and concrete effort values remain implementation details to verify before execution.
- Historical reference only: the public runner uses temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95, enables reasoning on supported models, and supplies no explicit output-token or reasoning-token cap. Its historical provider defaults and exact reasoning budgets are not fully pinned. The bounded motif-MCQ comparison below uses the agreed integration configuration, including its explicit 16,384-token cap; it does not recreate unspecified historical provider defaults.
- Do not add a tiny answer-token cap: the prompt requests visible analysis as well as a letter, and some APIs share the output budget between reasoning and final text. Use an initial shared cap of 16,384 total generated tokens per question across models, covering reasoning plus visible analysis and answer text. Report truncation rates by model and subtask; any later budget change defines a separately identified run configuration. Reuse context preflight and verify how each provider enforces the shared total. Where only independent hard caps exist, their allocations must sum to the shared total; allocation remains an open choice. Flag providers that cannot enforce a comparable limit rather than claiming equivalence.
- Where a provider supports independent reasoning and output controls, record both and their semantics. Do not assume `max_tokens` means final-answer-only tokens. Record effective request parameters, prompt/output/reasoning usage when available, finish reasons, and empty/reasoning-only/truncated response counts. Do not truncate input DNA to fit context or selectively rerun wrong answers with larger budgets.
- Verify the agreed GenomeQA settings after model/evaluation configuration is resolved. At Marin `fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3`, [`config_for()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L126-L165) uses the lower of the model and benchmark token limits, so a model cannot raise the benchmark cap but can lower it. Model generation arguments still merge last and can override sampling. Reuse this existing cap protection; add scoped validation of the agreed 16,384 allowance and 0.7/0.95 sampling, retaining explicit provider exceptions and model-specific reasoning controls. Do not silently change precedence for unrelated benchmarks. Test conflicting higher/lower model caps and sampling values, then inspect the actual provider request before execution. [Policy #10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) has benchmark-specific thinking overrides; provider defaults are not a universal existing rule.

Carbon comparison:

The [Carbon-X model card](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X) reports temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, thinking disabled, and one sample per problem. Its [public evaluator](https://github.com/huggingface/carbon/blob/4ca3ce3e5c55e5821d6068bac5c6e3806027a26f/carbon-x/evaluation/evaluate.py) reads local-model sampling settings from `generation_config.json`; endpoint sampling arguments default to unset unless overridden. This verifies public defaults, not every historical API run's payload. For local GenomeQA, its default output budget is context length minus 17,408 prompt tokens (23,552 for a 40,960 context).

Carbon's [GenomeQA task](https://github.com/huggingface/carbon/blob/4ca3ce3e5c55e5821d6068bac5c6e3806027a26f/carbon-x/evaluation/tasks/genomeqa.py) uses Inspect's `multiple_choice(cot=True)`, `choice()` scorer, and equal-weight subtask accuracy on the modified MCQ dataset distributed through `DNAIntelligenceIndex`. It does not install the original optimized system prompt. Its reported score is therefore not a parity target for this original-data, original-prompt integration. A Carbon-protocol comparison would be a separate evaluation.

Implementation split (approved after review of draft PR #10984):

- Keep [PR #10984](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10984) focused on the adapter and registration. Reuse the existing weighted means, tagged groups, response extraction, and runtime sample/resume machinery. Remove the proposed generic reducer, reducer-schema additions, helper relocation, Marin ingestion changes, and dashboard changes from this PR.
- Apply weight 5 to motif questions and weight 1 to other questions for `genomeqa_macro` only. Every cell then has equal total weight. Keep `accuracy` unweighted for actual correct counts. Tagged groups retain six subtask macros, BCQ/MCQ macros, 12 cell accuracies, and counts in saved results. This replaces the earlier custom-reducer proposal.
- Keep effective generation validation inside the source. Reject arbitrary limited populations; the dedicated motif-MCQ task evaluates its entire 100-question cell. The two runtime policy opt-ins score completed empty responses and withhold aggregates when any question is ungraded; other benchmarks retain their existing behavior. Failed-run samples and coverage remain available for inspection and resume.
- Follow up separately with dashboard subtask columns, native ingestion/reporting validation, and public sample-access restrictions. Do not expose GenomeQA runs in public dashboard records before those restrictions are implemented. The reporting requirements remain part of this issue.

Implementation scope:

Target Marin's vendored Evalchemy at [`vendor/evalchemy`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/vendor/evalchemy). Current `main`, checked at `fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3`, includes this runtime. Loom's cited `44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e` describes an older external-fork architecture; a separate fork PR and dependency pin are not required by the current layout.

1. Add one GenomeQA implementation for both pinned HF formats in `vendor/evalchemy`, preserving text, option order, composite IDs, and prompt layout without answer leakage. Reuse existing dataset loading, generated-answer execution, response handling, shared extraction, and durable output/resume components. Verify available interfaces before introducing helpers.
2. Add final-answer selection and the 12-cell reduction with all denominators, six subtask scores, BCQ/MCQ summaries, and the overall macro. Gate complete scores on expected coverage; retain partial diagnostics. [`SourceMetrics`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/vendor/evalchemy/eval/execution/metrics.py) already accumulates tagged group means/counts, but its default headline is a pooled mean and `weighted_macro` specifically consumes WildBench `adjusted_score` fields. Use the existing per-metric weighted mean and tagged groups, with runtime full-coverage gating; do not use the WildBench-specific reducer or derive a solved count as macro × 5,200. Preserve actual per-item correct counts.
3. Add portable configuration and Marin registry entries. Validate effective generation settings as described above and verify provider requests. Keep model-specific reasoning controls explicit.
4. Verify the current FineStore path through Marin ingestion and EvalDash. [`read_evalchemy_outcome()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L345) uses `FineStoreEvalchemyResult` and native sample summaries; the result-tree reader is retained for historical artifacts. Declare the primary macro metric and all reporting metrics through `BenchmarkMetadata`/`BaseBenchmark` metadata, including source names, kinds, and expected population. Test canonical metrics and coverage through the actual FineStore reader, record construction, and dashboard measurement path, not only a legacy `results_*.json` fixture. The dashboard currently produces one headline per evaluation record; extra scalar metrics alone do not create six subtask columns. Implement explicit reporting views from the same generated outputs, preserving overall, six primary subtask scores, secondary summaries, and 12 cells without rerunning questions or double-counting coverage. Preserve the macro value rather than substituting pooled accuracy, and do not attach a pooled-binomial interval to an unequal-cell macro; reuse the existing measurement handling for scores that are not a single correct/total ratio.
5. Register prompt-length metadata alongside the source. The current [`prompt-length contract`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3/vendor/evalchemy/tests/contracts/test_prompt_length.py) requires each registered custom benchmark to have a measurement or an explicit unmeasured reason. Measure the original rendered prompts with the existing tool, and verify actual model/provider context capacity separately. Keep `max_tokens: 16384` explicit: `resolve_task_max_tokens()` otherwise derives a budget from spare context when metadata is available. Do not copy GraphWalks' context-dependent question filtering or per-item budget policy; its bounded Parquet loading is reusable, but GenomeQA retains the pinned full population and shared cap.

The [LAB-Bench proposal](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10575) and [related PR #10582](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10582) remain separate work; LAB-Bench has not been approved as Marin evaluation policy. It may supply implementation ideas but is not an adopted-policy precedent or a prerequisite for GenomeQA.

Validation proposal:

- Reproduce the pinned data comparison and exact prompt rendering; verify parser behavior for BCQ/MCQ, misleading letters in analysis, missing final output, and truncation. Verify macro versus micro aggregation with unequal family sizes, a missing example, and an entirely missing cell. Verify that truncated responses score zero even when they contain an answer, while transport failures remain ungraded. Check resume identity across formats and subtasks. Include regression coverage for conflicting model generation settings and a FineStore artifact fixture passed through native ingestion, canonical metadata, record construction, and dashboard measurement to verify metric identities and coverage. Cover all-empty completed responses, missing cells, and a fixture where macro and micro differ; verify actual correct counts and prevent a spurious pooled-binomial interval for the macro.
- First-pass live validation: select all 100 rows with `subtask == "6_motif"` from the pinned HF `mcq` file. Use `meta-llama/llama-4-maverick` through OpenRouter, with a pinned provider, the original prompt, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, one response per question, and the agreed 16,384-token total cap. Maverick uses ordinary generation because it has no separate thinking mode. DigitalOcean is the current low-cost candidate; verify availability and limits before execution.
- Compare observed correct/100 with Llama-4’s **65.0%** TF-motif MCQ entry in [paper Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.05774v1#S4.T2). Retain all per-question outputs and report uncertainty, parse failures, truncations, infrastructure failures, actual cost, and runtime. If any question remains ungraded, label the result partial rather than claiming a complete-cell comparison. Do not select retries or change settings based on wrong answers.
- This validates one complete cell, not all 12 cells or the full aggregate. Its short sequences do not establish long-input handling. Provider/version differences, stochastic sampling, the adapted parser, and our explicit output cap limit historical reproducibility; matching 65.0% is not an acceptance gate. Offline data/prompt checks must still cover every cell. Additional live coverage and any full-benchmark run require separate scope.
Licensing and asset handling decision:

- Continue implementing our own loader, parser, and scoring code without making an author reply a prerequisite. Do not copy upstream implementation code or vendor benchmark questions into Marin. Fetch only the pinned HF files at runtime, retaining revision and checksums.
- The authors' current GitHub repository has no declared license, and the HF card has no dataset license. Record the dataset license as unspecified; do not label it Apache-2.0 or CC BY by inheritance. Runtime download does not itself grant dataset-use permission.
- The [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05774) is CC BY 4.0, but its Figure 8 prompt differs from the pinned runner. The comparison found omissions including the explicit binary-choice letter instruction, the rule for interpreting multiple simultaneous features, and some wording in the reasoning protocol. The decision is to keep using the runner prompt externally, pinned to the original commit, and record its hash. Fetch the source as data and extract only the literal prompt string without executing the module. Do not bundle the runner prompt or substitute Figure 8 silently. This supersedes the earlier proposal to source an equivalent prompt from the paper.
- The paper describes the code and data as available and the underlying databases as open for academic/research purposes. This supports the intended research context but does not establish an explicit license for the assembled dataset or separate code release. This implementation decision does not claim those rights are settled.
- Use synthetic questions in checked-in tests. Keep downloaded questions and raw request/response artifacts needed for reproducibility in controlled run storage. Public issue/PR reports and dashboard exports should use IDs, aggregate metrics, and diagnostics without question text; account for question text echoed in model responses as well. Dataset redistribution requires a separate decision if terms become available.
- This decision does not expand the agreed live evaluation scope or remove the requirement to pin provider settings and cost/time bounds before the 100-question run.

Done when the vendored Evalchemy implementation and Marin integration are reviewable at a recorded revision; the source, prompt, extraction, effective settings, aggregation, and report/dashboard mapping are reviewable; offline checks pass and the scoped 100-question first-pass comparison is documented with durable evidence; the overall and six primary subtask scores retain the secondary BCQ/MCQ summaries, 12 component results, and coverage. Matching the paper’s score and full-benchmark parity are not acceptance requirements. Implementation is distinct from admission into the official evaluation policy.

issues.body:
The hero GB200 canary timed out in Actions after 340 minutes without starting training. Kueue kept all 16 training tasks gated, while the monitor treated the child job's `RUNNING` state as proof that training had started and disabled its 18,000-second queue timeout. The metric report never ran. Classification: **infra/scheduling**.

Reproduce:
1. Submit a 16-task GB200 gang whose Kueue workload waits for admission. The child job becomes `RUNNING` while its tasks remain `BUILDING`.
2. In `scripts/ci/iris_monitor.py`, `_child_started` returns true for the child job's `RUNNING` state; `wait_for_child_job` drops the queue deadline. The Actions step then reaches its 340-minute timeout.

Expected: The queue deadline remains active until a training task starts. On expiry, the configured `shutdown` policy cancels the parent and reports a resource-exhaustion skip.

<details>
<summary>Evidence</summary>

- [Actions wait step](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/41692115065/job/126113066350) logged `Child ... reached RUNNING; dropping queue timeout` at 22:34:11 UTC and `The action 'Wait for hero canary' has timed out after 340 minutes` at 04:13:22 UTC.
- Iris task `/runner/hero-canary-41692115065-1-coord/grug-train-hero-canary-41692115065-1/0` remained `BUILDING`: `SchedulingGated ... Kueue workload iris-pg-f81e996a053a07ba-0: queue=cw-use08a-lq; waiting for Kueue admission`.
- Finelog `marin`, `iris.task_state`, root job `/runner/hero-canary-41692115065-1-coord`: all 679 samples from 22:34:46 to 04:13:36 UTC show `building=16`, `assigned=0`, `running=1` (the coordinator). The uploaded [diagnostics artifact](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/41692115065/artifacts/13294544130) has no training task output.
- The [monitor predicate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8fd094fd23f0fd5b6992244c87f10a5bd99f49e3/scripts/ci/iris_monitor.py#L119-L123) reads only the child job state. A local call with child `RUNNING` and task counts `BUILDING=16`, `RUNNING=0` returns `True`.

</details>

## Canary run context

- Lane: `hero-gb200`
- Job ID: `/runner/hero-canary-41692115065-1-coord`
- GHA run: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/41692115065
- W&B run URL: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-canary-41692115065-1 (training did not start)

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
One SWE-bench Verified trial in the 2026-11-04 eval campaign (model Contributor-Plain, trial `django__django-10880__Wspb9gU`) finished its agent phase at 22:51Z on Nov 4 and never reached verification. At 09:12Z on Nov 5 the stage still reported 499/500 completed and 1 running, with no terminal record. The campaign runs the seven Harbor benchmarks serially per model inside one group, so the six benchmarks queued behind SWE could not start. The group had to be stopped and the remaining six relaunched; the SWE score was reconstructed from the 499 per-trial `result.json` files.

Why nothing fired:

- Harbor's `Trial._await_phase` bounds `agent.run` only (agent 1800 s, verifier 300 s, agent setup 360 s, environment build 1800 s). The `finally` block that syncs agent output and the artifact work after it are outside every phase bound. The verifier timeout is not armed until verification starts.
- `trial_attempt` timeout resolves to null in the campaign's job and trial config, so there is no whole-trial deadline either.
- Stopping the trial's sandbox from outside (Daytona SDK stop, then 404 on get) did not unblock the driver: the stage still showed 499 at 09:12Z. Trial cancellation is not exposed; the trial is an async task inside the shared driver.

This is a different mechanism from #10608, where leftover Pi processes make the verifier time out. Here the verifier never starts and no timeout is armed.

Reproduce:
1. Launch a campaign Harbor group with the standard config (`experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/`, `launch-campaign.sh --harbor`).
2. Make one trial hang between agent completion and verification (for example, stall the sandbox during output sync).
3. Observe the stage never finalizes and the remaining benchmarks in the group never start.

Expected: every trial has a wall-clock deadline that covers the whole attempt, not only the agent phase. When it fires the trial is recorded as an infrastructure error, the stage finalizes with that trial missing, and the next benchmark in the group starts.

Evidence (sanitized, on the campaign host): `plain-swe-timeout-and-reconstruction-findings-r1.json` (sha256 7cd7c5d2…); native job config sha256 46ca2aaf…, trial config sha256 c09a9ce8….

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The eight campaign Harbor policies leave `trial_attempt_timeout_sec` unset, so the admitted attempt has no deadline while output sync runs outside the agent phase. The vendored Harbor queue already selects and persists a `TrialTimeoutError` when this deadline expires, but the campaign allows ten retries of that error; adding only a deadline could repeat the stall eleven times.

**Relevant code**
- [`swebench-verified.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ca7f3f4bdd37a8075aaf16a75908014c9be2798/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/harbor-configs/swebench-verified.yaml#L1-L21) — missing deadline and retry policy
- [`queue.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ca7f3f4bdd37a8075aaf16a75908014c9be2798/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/queue.py#L325-L353) — admitted-attempt supervision
- [`common.sh`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ca7f3f4bdd37a8075aaf16a75908014c9be2798/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/common.sh#L447-L460) — campaign config checks

# Proposed Fix

Set a 5400-second attempt deadline in all eight campaign policies. The configured build, setup, agent, and verifier caps total 4260 seconds; 1140 seconds remain for output sync and cleanup. Remove `TrialTimeoutError` from the infrastructure retry allowlist so a timed-out attempt is recorded once, and make `validate-campaign.sh` reject policies missing either constraint. Verify that a stalled output sync yields a terminal trial result and lets the next serial benchmark start.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 PR #10963 sets a 5400-second deadline for each campaign Harbor attempt and removes `TrialTimeoutError` from the retry allowlist, so an expired attempt is recorded once. Campaign preflight and the focused Harbor tests pass. The broader local test run stopped because this sandbox's Python lacks `os.pidfd_open`; the original Daytona sync stall was not reproduced locally.

comments.body:
🤖 Specifics for reproducing or inspecting the two stalls seen so far (both on Marin main 8d789914 + d21aaea1, campaign launcher `experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/launch-campaign.sh --harbor`, records under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/`).

**Occurrence 1: Contributor-Plain, SWE-bench Verified, 2026-11-04**

- Run id `20261104-210107-open-athena-Snowball-67B-A2B-SFT-Shootout-Contributor-Plain-v0.1-2026.10.22-88b06fac34044a0c9af634f318294c1d-swebench-verified-72cf1117f678516dbe5770f60f3cf93a` ([EvalDash runs for this model](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs?model=open-athena-Snowball-67B-A2B-SFT-Shootout-Contributor-Plain-v0.1-2026.10.22)).
- Stuck trial `django__django-10880__Wspb9gU`: agent phase started 22:49:05Z, finished 22:51Z, never verified. Stage stats stayed 499 completed / 1 running from 22:51Z (Nov 4) through 09:12Z (Nov 5).
- Resolved timeouts in the trial config: agent 1800, verifier 300, agent setup 360, environment build 1800, cleanup grace 30, `trial_attempt` null.
- Stopping the trial's Daytona sandbox from outside at ~09:06Z returned, but the stage still reported 499 at 09:12Z.
- Outcome: the root was stopped; the six remaining benchmarks were relaunched as a separate group (`20261105-093017-open-athena-Snowball-67B-A2B-SFT-Shootout-Contributor-Plain-v0.1-2026.10.22-cd75b4fdeb914d04bf800ef9e359f70a`); the SWE cell was reconstructed from the 499 per-trial `result.json` files (142 passes, 1 infra NULL). Receipt: [plain--swebench-verified.json](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/ec3578ee2beb0f7752afe17b7a13b6ebc122bce8/eval-policy-2026-11-04/receipts/plain--swebench-verified.json).

**Occurrence 2: MixedRS-SFT-Step727, SWE-bench Verified, 2026-11-05**

- Run id `20261104-210729-open-athena-Snowball-67B-A2B-MixedRS-SFT-Step727-194c1db076084ac3afaa4ba4fc3ac440-swebench-verified-fea38b1df66c5cb38141e3e09e6ee432` ([EvalDash runs for this model](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs?model=open-athena-Snowball-67B-A2B-MixedRS-SFT-Step727)).
- Stage started 22:02Z (Nov 4); last trial finished 22:01:23Z (Nov 5); stats 499 completed / 1 running / 74 errored / 174 retries, executor still RUNNING at 23:06Z (Nov 5).
- Stuck trial `astropy__astropy-12907__UR4UBan` on retry attempt 006. Note for anyone reading the stage by files: every one of the 500 trial directories carried a top-level `result.json`, because the retried trial keeps the previous attempt's file at the top level; the in-flight trial is the one whose newest `attempts/NNN/` has no `result.json`. Counting top-level files says 500/500 while the stats say 499/500.
- Outcome: time-boxed at 23:06Z, root stopped once, the six remaining benchmarks submitted as parallel groups.

**Where the deadlines live** (main 1ca7f3f4bd)

- [`_run_agent_phase`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ca7f3f4bdd37a8075aaf16a75908014c9be2798/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L622-L700): only `agent.run` sits inside `_await_phase`; the cleanup `finally` and the output sync after it do not.
- [`_await_phase`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ca7f3f4bdd37a8075aaf16a75908014c9be2798/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L720-L795): the per-phase bound.
- [`_sync_agent_output`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ca7f3f4bdd37a8075aaf16a75908014c9be2798/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L1129): the post-agent work with no bound of its own.
- [`trial_attempt_timeout_sec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ca7f3f4bdd37a8075aaf16a75908014c9be2798/vendor/harbor/src/harbor_config/models/trial/config.py#L444): the whole-attempt deadline the campaign policies leave unset (PR #10963 sets it).

Both stalls hit the longest benchmark in the serial group, so each cost the arm roughly a day of wall clock before the stop-and-relaunch. Sanitized readings (stage stats, trial bindings, timeout resolution) are on the campaign host under `/mnt/storage/karan-scratchpad/`; ask in this thread for a specific file.

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
### Slurm wrapper used by every command in this issue

All commands submit `run_gpu.sh` from `$WORK/marin` on the AMD HPC Fund cluster. It turns XLA command buffers off; a later `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=...` in `XLA_FLAGS` overrides that. It will be committed to the repo; this comment is the reference until then.

<details><summary>run_gpu.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -o pipefail
cd "$WORK/marin"
export RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=${RAGGED_DOT_IMPL:-xla} PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Command buffers (HIP graphs) corrupt memory on this ROCm stack: nan gradients and segfaults after a few steps.
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer= $XLA_FLAGS"
uv run --no-sync python "$@" 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered -v -E "rocm_pcie_bandwidth|rocm_executor"
```

</details>

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

comments.body:
🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,229 TFLOP/s in JAX by kernel time (53% of datasheet peak, 97% of PyTorch's sustained 1,261)

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421), 6b47d18 (JAX 454529), 370d41d (JAX 454561), 704ceff (JAX 454577-454580) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt and rocBLAS; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every rocBLAS and hipBLASLt solution per shape and keeps the fastest) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load. It times each `torch.mm` with GPU events recorded just before and after the call, so its rates count kernel time only.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. It runs under `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` and reports two rates per shape. Kernel time divides the FLOPs by the GPU time of the kernels inside each window, which matches MAMF-finder's timing. Wall clock divides them by host time, which also counts host dispatch and the idle GPU time between calls. Both are sustained rates, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare with.

Hardware and theoretical peaks:

| | MI350X | MI300X |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture, compute units | gfx950, 256 CUs | gfx942, 304 CUs |
| Memory per GPU (as torch reports it) | 288 GB HBM3E (294,896 MB) | 192 GB HBM3 (196,592 MB) |
| Dense bf16 and fp16 peak | 2,307 TFLOP/s, as in this issue (brochure: 2,309.6) | 1,307 TFLOP/s (datasheet: 1,307.4) |
| Node, Slurm partition | k007-002, `mi3508x` | k002-003, `mi3008x` |

The peaks are AMD's dense figures without structured sparsity. `lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py` stores the brochure values; the percentages below use 2,307 and 1,307 to match the tables above.

Software, identical on both GPUs:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ROCm user-space libraries | `rocm==10.0.0` wheels (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-libraries`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx942`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx950`) from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/` |
| hipBLASLt, rocBLAS | 100401-8d1ae90e, 5.6.0.8d1ae90e (from TunableOp's results file) |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, with `amd-torch-device-gfx942` and `-gfx950` 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0. `torch.version.hip` is 7.15.26333 and `torch.version.cuda` is None: a ROCm build, no CUDA |
| JAX | jax and jaxlib 0.11.0, `jax_rocm10_plugin` and `jax_rocm10_pjrt` 0.11.0+rocm10.0.0 |
| Kernel tracing | `rocprofv3` from the `rocm-sdk-core` 10.0.0 wheel |
| MAMF-finder | commit [0359db8](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), benchmark version 4, auto search, default tuning |
| Python, OS | 3.12.12, Linux 5.14.0-611.54.1.el9_7 |
| JAX flags | `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`; the Triton-off run adds `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` |

Each run used GPU 0 while the other 7 GPUs on the node were idle.

```bash
sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/mamf.sbatch --dtype bfloat16"
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/jax_matmul.sbatch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --m-range 4096 20480 4096 --n-range 4096 20480 4096 --k-range 4096 20480 4096 \
  --shapes-file experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt"
```

Results in TFLOP/s per GPU, with the share of the dense peak. Shapes are MxNxK. The JAX column is kernel time, with the traced wall-clock rate of the same shape in parentheses.

| GPU | dtype | MAMF (PyTorch) | MSMF (PyTorch) | JAX best | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI350X | bf16 | 1,445 (62.6%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 (54.7%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,229 (53.3%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,178) | 453328, 454577 |
| MI350X | fp16 | 1,377 (59.7%) @ 4096x4096x20480 | 1,177 (51.0%) @ 8192x4096x14336 | 1,086 (47.1%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,047) | 453329, 454578 |
| MI300X | bf16 | 698 (53.4%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | 645 (49.3%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | not run | 453334 |

The JAX column covers a 125-shape grid (M, N and K each 4096, 8192, ..., 20480), the June model's projection shapes, and, for bf16, the 28 shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted (job 454579). By kernel time, JAX reaches 97% of MSMF in bf16 and 92% in fp16. Without the tracer, the best bf16 wall-clock rate was 1,192 at 4096x4096x16384 and 1,180 at 4096x4096x12288 (job 453420).

Measured against these ceilings instead of the datasheet, the MI350X baseline above (3.88% MFU, 90 TFLOP/s per GPU) runs at 7.3% of the JAX bf16 kernel-time ceiling. The confirmed MI300X batch-16 row (8.66%, 113 TFLOP/s) runs at 17.5% of PyTorch's MSMF; JAX was not measured on MI300X.

The MI300X run reproduces the MI300X bf16 row in [Stas Bekman's table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (MAMF 676, MSMF 659, PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0): MAMF is 3.3% higher and MSMF 2.1% lower. His table has no MI350X row. His MI355X row reads 62.6% of peak, the same share as our MI350X MAMF.

The next table times the same matmul shapes in both frameworks, in bf16 on MI350X, using the shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted. MSMF is PyTorch's sustained rate after TunableOp has kept the fastest rocBLAS or hipBLASLt solution for that shape; the TunableOp column names the library it picked. JAX kernel time comes from job 454579, where XLA's autotuner picked a hipBLASLt kernel for every shape. JAX wall clock comes from job 453412, which ran without the tracer.

| Shape | MSMF | TunableOp | JAX kernel | JAX / MSMF, kernel | JAX wall | JAX / MSMF, wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 | rocBLAS | 1,052 | 83% | 1,008 | 80% |
| 4096x4096x8192 | 1,246 | hipBLASLt | 1,209 | 97% | 1,150 | 92% |
| 3584x4608x8192 | 1,237 | rocBLAS | 1,199 | 97% | 1,137 | 92% |
| 4096x4096x20480 | 1,224 | hipBLASLt | 1,179 | 96% | 1,153 | 94% |
| 4096x2048x20480 | 1,089 | hipBLASLt | 1,111 | 102% | 1,065 | 98% |
| 2048x4096x4096 | 1,080 | rocBLAS | 959 | 89% | 828 | 77% |

An earlier version of this comment read the 2-23% wall-clock gap as XLA choosing slower kernels. Most of that gap was the timing method. Wall clock counts host dispatch and the GPU's idle time between calls: on MI350X a trivial jitted op takes about 43 µs to dispatch, and the GPU idles about 12-15 µs between executions even when the host keeps ahead (job 454529). Kernel time removes that overhead. On 2048x4096x4096 it moves JAX from 77% to 89% of MSMF, and on 4096x4096x8192 from 92% to 97%. JAX's kernels are within 4% of MSMF on four shapes. Two gaps remain: 17 points on 4608x4096x7168 and 11 points on 2048x4096x4096. TunableOp picked a rocBLAS solution for both. Every GEMM kernel XLA picked in these runs carries hipBLASLt's `UserArgs` naming, and we have not checked whether XLA's autotuner considers rocBLAS solutions or whether they account for those gaps. TunableOp also picked rocBLAS for 3584x4608x8192, where JAX's hipBLASLt kernel reaches 97%.

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's projection GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 369 TFLOP/s (k and v weight gradients, 2560x640x4096) to 1,058 (lm head weight gradient) by kernel time through JAX (job 454577). 4096x2560x2560 is the shape of the q, attention output and shared expert gate, up and down projections, and of their input gradients. It runs at 972 by kernel time and 826 by untraced wall clock (job 454529). The lm head forward runs at 1,030 by kernel time and 1,029 by untraced wall clock. The k and v projections, 4096x640x2560, run at 427 by kernel time with XLA's Triton GEMM and at 556 with hipBLASLt (next table). By untraced wall clock they run at 257 with Triton. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` and the small router, attention gate and GatedNorm GEMMs are not covered.

In bf16, XLA generates its own Triton GEMM for four of the k and v shapes: every shape with a dimension of 640, and 2560x1280x4096. Every other shape uses a hipBLASLt kernel. With `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` (job 454580), XLA uses hipBLASLt for these shapes too, and its kernels run 17-33% faster in bf16. Kernel time in TFLOP/s:

| Shape | Use | Triton (454577) | hipBLASLt, Triton off (454580) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096x640x2560 | k and v projections | 427 | 556 | +30% |
| 2560x640x4096 | k and v weight gradients | 369 | 490 | +33% |
| 2560x1280x4096 | k and v weight gradients, fused | 514 | 664 | +29% |
| 4096x2560x640 | k and v input gradients | 471 | 552 | +17% |

Of the other 38 shapes in the Triton-off run, 33 used the same hipBLASLt kernel as with Triton on, and their kernel time moved by at most 1.6%. For the other 5, the autotuner picked a different hipBLASLt kernel in the new run (see the variation note). Under the tracer, wall clock moved the other way on the four Triton shapes: on 4096x640x2560 a call took 48 µs with Triton and 61 µs with hipBLASLt, against kernel times of 31 and 24 µs, so host-side work sets the wall-clock rate at this size. We have not measured these shapes with Triton off without the tracer. In fp16 (job 454578), XLA also picks Triton for 4096x2560x1280; we did not run fp16 with Triton off.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- fp16 is slower than bf16 for dense matmuls on MI350X: MAMF is 5% lower, JAX 12% lower by kernel time.
- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,179 and 1,229 TFLOP/s by kernel time (job 454577).
- Run-to-run variation on k007-002. With the same kernel, repeated runs agree closely: across the 24 MAMF shapes where jobs 454579 and 454580 ran the same kernel, the median difference is 0.3% and the largest 0.6%. Some shapes move more. 4096x4096x16384 measured 1,188, 1,221 and 1,189 by kernel time (jobs 454529, 454561, 454577), and 1,192 and 1,153 by untraced wall clock (jobs 453420, 454529). Treat differences of about 3% as noise. XLA's autotuner can also pick a different hipBLASLt kernel for the same shape in a new run. It did so for 4 of the 28 MAMF shapes between jobs 454579 and 454580 and moved three of them by 7-12% (for example 20480x4096x12288: 1,039 with a 192x320 tile in job 454579, 1,164 with a 256x256 tile in job 454580).
- Under `rocprofv3`, wall clock reads lower for shapes that take less than about 100 µs per call, because the tracer adds host work to every dispatch: 4096x1280x2560 reads 401 traced (job 454561) and 472-550 in two untraced passes (job 454529). Wall-clock numbers above say which kind they are.
- The node matters. JAX on MAMF-finder's 28 shapes ran a median of 3% faster on k007-002 than on k007-004 by wall clock, and faster on 26 of the 28 shapes (jobs 453412 and 453338). The two slower shapes, 20480x4096x12288 (-8%) and 16384x8192x8192 (-4%), may reflect XLA's autotuner picking a different kernel rather than the node: 1,043 on k007-002 matches the 192x320-tile kernel in the variation note, and these two runs did not record kernel names. k007-001 and k007-003 have not been compared. The bf16 grid's best wall-clock rate was 1,156 on k007-004 (job 453314) against 1,192 on k007-002.
- With `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, JAX ran bf16 matmuls at 15-17 TFLOP/s, 1% of the autotuned rate (job 453316, stopped by its 45-minute limit after 99 shapes). Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The MI350X MAMF and MSMF runs (jobs 453328 and 453329) predate the fix in stas00/ml-engineering#143, so their power and clock readings, the 38 MHz and 308 W in their logs, and the "not a boost burst" warning from the MAMF boost check all come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86%, JAX by kernel time on the same shape (1,189 in job 454577) about 81%, and JAX by untraced wall clock in job 453523 (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.
- Next: measure a training step with `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` to see whether the faster hipBLASLt kernels for the k and v GEMMs carry over. Separately, check whether XLA can use the rocBLAS solutions TunableOp picked for 4608x4096x7168 and 2048x4096x4096 (`tunableop-*.csv` in the results directory), and whether those solutions close the remaining gaps.

</details>

Edit: first posted with JAX numbers from node k007-004 while MAMF-finder ran on k007-002. All MI350X numbers now come from k007-002. JAX medians now use the true median of the ten windows. The MI350X telemetry note was corrected after jobs 453520 and 453523 showed MAMF-finder sampling a different GPU. Second edit: JAX now reports kernel time from a `rocprofv3` trace next to wall clock, and comparisons with MAMF and MSMF use kernel time (jobs 454577-454580). This corrects the earlier reading that the wall-clock gap came from XLA's kernel choice; XLA's choice still costs 17-33% on the k and v shapes, where it picks its own Triton GEMM. The Snowball shapes now cover separate k and v projections, the k and v weight gradients and the input gradients, and the paragraph names every projection behind a shared shape. Added the Triton-off comparison, the run-to-run variation note, and the TunableOp library choices. Scripts moved to `experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/`, and the grid arguments are now `--m-range`, `--n-range` and `--k-range`.

| 2.426 s (was 2.634) | 108,100 (was 99,500) | 9.32% (was 8.58%) | 184.2 GiB (unchanged) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Loss matches the baseline to 4 decimals (11.7770 vs 11.7769 at step 19).
- Forward and dlhs now launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a device-side tile map, instead of a full row grid per expert. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. drhs uses an explicit flat grid. Rows past the last group are zero-filled.

  | Layout | w13 | w2 |
  |---|---|---|
  | fwd | 583 → 722 | 555 → 667 |
  | dlhs | 554 → 760 | 538 → 757 |
  | drhs | 410 → 581 | 396 → 573 |

- At batch 64 the tile map alone changes nothing. With the old blocks, w13 forward takes 2.95 ms either way. The gain there is block tuning. At batch 8 the tile map is a 4.6× win.
- `plgpu.CompilerParams` exposes only `num_warps` and `num_stages`, so AMD knobs (`waves_per_eu`, `matrix_instr_nonkdim`, `kpack`) can't be set from Pallas.
- drhs, at 573–581 TFLOP/s, is the remaining gap. Both of its operands are contraction-strided.

  - With every matmul at the 1,156 TFLOP/s JAX ceiling, the step would be about 1.34 s, about 17% MFU.
- GPU 0, ms per step (recompute_all / save_moe):

  | Module | recompute_all | save_moe |
  |---|---|---|
  | MoE expert Triton `ragged_dot` | 431 | 344 |
  | flash attention kernels | 244 | 245 |
  | synchronous collectives | 214 | 161 |
  | shared expert MLP | 172 | 122 |
  | block glue (residuals, converts, copies) | 164 | 191 |
  | MoE dispatch/combine (`input_scatter_fusion` 114) | 150 | 147 |
  | loss and lm head | 119 | 120 |
  | q/k/v/o projections (about 1,070 TFLOP/s) | 104 | 105 |
  | optimizer (Adam) and outside fwd/bwd | 100 | 116 |
  | routing (40 / 37 of rocprim sorts) | 53 | 49 |

- Flash attention:
  - forward and remat run at 346-350 TFLOP/s on the FLOPs the mask needs, dQ at 300-310 and dK/dV at 193-197
  - dK/dV takes 111 ms per step, the weakest large kernel
- `ragged_dot` per call:
  - fwd w13 at 725-733 TFLOP/s, fwd w2 (K=1280) at 555-561, dlhs at 670-872
  - drhs at 447-498, below the 573-581 of the microbenchmark: 135-145 ms per step
- Exposed collectives:
  - recompute_all: 214 ms synchronous:
    - forward EP reduce-scatter 109 (26 × 4.2 ms)
    - per-layer gradient all-reduces 60
    - remat reduce-scatter 19
    - routing all-gather 19
  - save_moe: 161 ms synchronous: backward EP all-gather 96 and gradient all-reduces 57. Another 94 ms of backward reduce-scatter is unhidden.
  - Estimated unprofiled exposed time: about 255 ms (recompute_all) and about 335 ms (save_moe).
  - The shared expert MLP is what hides the async EP traffic: 140 of its 152 ms of GEMMs run under a collective with recompute_all, but only 41 with save_moe.

- Next, by estimated unprofiled saving (MFU from the 1.837 s save_moe step):
  1. token-deduplicated EP dispatch: 100-170 ms (13.0-13.6%); high effort
  2. a gather-based MoE combine, starting with an f32-buffer test: 60-85 ms (12.7-12.9%); low effort
  3. hide the synchronous EP collectives, with the shared-expert backward under them for save_moe or a chunked MoE pipeline for recompute_all: 50-90 ms; overlaps with item 1
  4. `ragged_dot` drhs and fwd w2 tiles: 55-75 ms
  5. retile flash dK/dV: about 40 ms (an AITER/CK kernel: 110-120 ms, 3-5 days)
  6. one gradient all-reduce after the scan: 35-45 ms
  7. a Pallas top-k for routing: 30-40 ms
  8. optimizer fusion: 40-55 ms (Adam in the benchmark; production uses MuonH)
  9. launch overhead: at most about 45 ms; skip

  Items 2 and 4-7 are independent and together reach about 1.55-1.62 s (14.0-14.6%).

</details>

🤖 Matmul-alone time in the MI350X `--overlap` runs (jobs 453572, 453633, 453651) takes one of two values between runs: about 2.46 ms in `min64`, `ring`, `prio-on` and `lhs-prio-off`, and about 2.88 ms in the other 16. The faster overlap rows of `min64`, `ring` and `prio-on` (all-gather 5.68 ms against 6.05 ms in `base`) match that matmul gap, so they do not show an effect of the RCCL or XLA setting. Details: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9886#issuecomment-6047294744

Because the variance is between processes, re-timing the matmul inside a run does not remove it. To compare settings, run each setting in several processes, interleave them, and compare medians of a per-run ratio such as the hidden fraction `(t_collective + t_matmul − t_both) / min(t_collective, t_matmul)`, using the matmul-alone time of the same run.
