What the data say:
- On identical tasks, GLM LOW rows push the student far below the parent, and contributor rows lift it above the parent on SWE-bench. The contributor-side +10 is the first gap against the parent that clears noise.
- Less GLM data does not help. lowshared used 39% of LOW plain's tokens and is not closer to the parent; 85 of its 100 SWE-bench episodes hit the context limit and it submitted 12 times. A lower learning rate (3e-7: SWE −7 [−13, −1] against 1e-6) and an earlier checkpoint (2 of 3 epochs: +5 [−4, +13]) also did not rescue the GLM rows.
- On contributor rows, plain, RS-multi, recovery and plateau dropping are indistinguishable.
- Limits: single runs on 100 tasks; the pair is matched on tasks, not tokens; read the small-budget pair for the gap, not for absolute levels.

Not tested: what remains between the row sets is the teacher (GLM 5.3 against Kimi/Qwen) and the harness format. Our GLM rows use each eval's own action protocol; the contributor rows use the other one.

Trace decontamination: the trained trace text was checked against the 100 SWE-bench gold and test patches and the 100 TBLite tests and solutions. There were 3 flags, all TBLite, all generic code (imports, a file-reading loop). Nothing was excluded.

Cost of these runs: 184.9 H100-h training and 106.4 H100-h screens. Documented total for the experiment: about 6,070 H100-h (a partial subtotal, not an invoice).

comments.author: karansag
comments.body: 🤖 **Summary: no SFT method beat plain SFT by enough to matter; the source of the traces decided the result. The experiment is stopped and written up.** ## Data We took 2,200 TMAX and 2,100 SWE-smith tasks and regenerated traces using GLM 5.3. This way, both would have a consistent teacher. We also ran these traces using the corresponding eval harness under policy. For SWE-smith, this was `mini-swe-agent`, and for TMax, it was `Terminus-2`. Relay pools were also constructed similarly, starting with a base Snowball and handing off to GLM 5.3 Note that GLM 5.3 was tried with different effort levels (as per comments above). We used the contributor rows directly (SWE-smith + TMax under Kimi 2.5 / Qwen3.6-27B) for both pilot sweeps and as a final run to assess the impact of our data after a negative with GLM 5.3 traces. ## What we did We compared plain SFT, rejection-sampled SFT (RS-multi), relay, recovery and plateau dropping for agentic coding on Snowball v0 and v0.1. The task pool was about 2,200 TMax and 2,100 SWE-smith tasks. Traces came from GLM 5.3 at three reasoning efforts, then from the contributor traces (Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith, Qwen3.6-27B TMax). Screens: SWE-bench Verified random-100, TBLite-100, GSM8K and BFCL-Parity. ## What we found 1. **Every arm trained on GLM 5.3 traces scored below its parent** on SWE-bench and TBLite, while gaining on GSM8K and BFCL. The students took about twice the steps of their training traces, ran into the 32k context limit in most SWE-bench episodes and rarely submitted. 2. **Methods mattered little.** Only relay on LOW rows beat plain SFT (SWE-bench +8 [+1, +16]), and it still trailed its parent. On contributor rows, plain, RS-multi, recovery and plateau dropping were indistinguishable. 3. **The rows mattered most.** With the same 1,432 tasks, parent and recipe, contributor rows beat GLM LOW rows by SWE-bench +26 [+17, +36] and TBLite +9 [+1, +17]. The contributor side also beat parent v0.1 on SWE-bench by +10 [+1, +19]. 4. **Less GLM exposure did not help.** A lower learning rate, an earlier checkpoint and a smaller subset all stayed below the parent. ## Hypotheses (untested) Why the GLM arms lost while the contributor rows gained, and why collaborators got large SFT gains from Kimi and Qwen traces on a weaker Snowball parent ([blog post, 2026-10-21](https://lukedhlee.github.io/blog/2026/10/21/turning-snowball-into-a-coding-agent/)). Ordered by how much evidence we have. 1. **Teacher traces.** GLM 5.3 episodes were long, reasoning-heavy and often ended at the context limit; the students copied that. Kimi and Qwen traces did not. The matched pair (+26 SWE-bench on the same tasks) is the strongest evidence we have for anything. A different teacher on the same tasks and format would test it. 2. **SFT alone does not fix action behavior.** The collaborators' best results came from SFT then RL; their trace analysis found RL cut invalid actions from about 80% to 2% and taught the model to submit its best effort instead of running out of context. Those are exactly the failures of our GLM students. RL from a shootout checkpoint would test it. 3. **Training stack.** The collaborators report that an early relay advantage disappeared after correcting training precision and MoE expert capacity. Our arms trained before #10492 made expert capacity configurable; at the default capacity with expert parallelism, overflow tokens are dropped silently (seen later in the identity work). Whether the shootout arms dropped tokens is not known. It can be checked by replaying one saved run with drop counting. 4. **Eval protocol.** Our screens use 32k context, 1,800 s and one trial; the collaborators use 64k, a 3x timeout and three repeats. Our GLM students produce longer episodes, so our limits may punish them more than a longer protocol would. The 65k-context and 5,400 s checks ran on the parent only, not on a student. 5. **Parent headroom.** Their parent was the general-SFT 09-21 checkpoint (12.8% SWE-bench under Terminus-2). Ours were merged and RL-trained parents, and v0 already carries a relay graft trained on 1,012 of the same Kimi trajectories. Demonstrations may have less to add to our parents. 6. **Harness format.** Our GLM traces were recorded in each eval's own harness and hurt that eval; the contributor traces were recorded the other way round and did not. Training in the eval's own format may overwrite the parent's behavior there. But the collaborators' Kimi SWE traces are Terminus-2 format and their SWE eval runs under Terminus-2, and that worked, so this is weaker than it first looked. Format is confounded with the teacher. Re-recording GLM traces in the other format (about 125 H100-h) would separate them. 7. **Training dose.** We trained 3 epochs at 1e-6. The collaborators' RL started from a 7-epoch SFT model, and their RL ablation found more epochs helped until overfitting. This would not rescue the GLM arms, which got worse, but the contributor rows were never trained past 3 epochs. Cost: about 6,070 H100-h documented. ## Records - Paper (15 pages, PDF, with the three experiment diagrams): [agentic-sft-shootout.pdf](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/f0ad30e1ebafa432c3af144aa6faad76119a6c97/logbooks/10213-sft-shootout/agentic-sft-shootout.pdf), with a short [notebook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/f0ad30e1ebafa432c3af144aa6faad76119a6c97/logbooks/10213-sft-shootout/notebook.md) and the diagram sources in marin-logbooks. - Results by round: the comments above, last two dated 2026-10-22 and 2026-10-24. - Code: reusable parts in draft PRs #10255 (plateau dropping in `train_lm`), #10887 (recording relay proxy and trace rebuild) and #10888 (recovery rows). The rest of the experiment code is archived on marin-logbooks branches `codex/10213-sft-shootout-pr`, listed in the notebook. - Models: private `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-SFT-Shootout-*` repos on the Hub.

spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

The one-sequence profile repeated all 100 fixed-panel results in six evaluations.
A separate concurrent candidate repeated all 100 results in four independently
graded passes, with different answers and mean reward. The concurrent candidate
requires separate runtime integration and qualification before adoption. Neither
finite panel establishes universal determinism; the exact #10760 head has not
been run on GPUs.

## Description

Record the fixed100 serving reproducibility experiments behind [#10760](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10760). The goal is exact agreement under repeated fresh processes and scheduling changes while retaining compilation and CUDA graphs.

## Fixed-panel serving profiles

The fixed panel contains 80 script-graded and 20 VerifyIt tasks from the canonical task-selection artifact. Each task retains its own grader and score range; mean reward averages the per-task normalized score.

The evaluations used Datakit SFT revision
`fe666478454e79fe6027a0bab0388d9abd68f51a` and its matching tokenizer.

The checked-in inventory recipe enables batch-invariant arithmetic, fixes the
evaluation seed to `20261020`, disables prefix caching, and limits each inference
worker to one scheduled sequence. It retains DP8/EP8/TP1/PP1, chunked prefill
with an 8,192-token scheduling budget, and CUDA graphs. The sequence cap also
applies to training generation and reduces concurrency. Training throughput
has not been measured.

Two runtime profiles have reproduced the fixed 100-task panel. They use different
runtime revisions and produce different answers; their scores are not a
controlled comparison of serving policies.

| Profile | Evidence | Exact agreement | Mean reward | Response tokens per pass |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One scheduled sequence; vLLM `39e62869693c` | Six evaluations across four fresh engine startups: four direct SFT and two Megatron initial evaluations | 100/100 tasks | 0.2002 | 469,450 |
| Concurrency-enabled scheduling; corrected vLLM `02872a7e5530` candidate, Torch 2.14.1+cu132 | Four fresh direct-SFT evaluation processes across two eight-H100 jobs on 2026-11-05 | 100/100 tasks | 0.1801 | 503,697 |

Agreement covers prompt and response token IDs and text, grades, verifier
outcomes, recorded operational outcomes, and reported aggregates. Recorded outcomes cover stop reason, exception/error treatment, server error, environment class, data source and environment metrics; this equality claim excludes timings and request IDs. Each pass
independently attempted and graded all 100 tasks. Missing grades, errors,
nonfinite values, or any compared-field mismatch fail the check; equal mean
scores alone do not pass it. The one-sequence Megatron evaluations used NCCL
`expert_block` weight transfer and exited before any optimizer step.

### Concurrent DP8/EP8 qualification

The four-pass concurrent qualification used the Datakit SFT checkpoint
and tokenizer recorded above, the original 24,576-token context and 8,192-token reply
limit, greedy decoding with seed `20261020`, and the original task-owned graders.
All 400 results were independently graded, verified and finite. There were zero
task-level or aggregate differences. Evaluation logprobs were not requested.
The worker sequence limit was 1,024; prefix caching stayed off, while TRITON
attention, 8,192-token chunked prefill and compilation/CUDA graphs stayed enabled.

This candidate used vLLM `02872a7e55304d288e52fdb906923551b9517501` plus
the [three IEEE FP32 Triton dot corrections](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/bf31042cab99d9d15eb5aa321d37c82fe4bcaf72)
in `batch_invariant.py`, now tracked in
[vLLM #117](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/117), with these native
TorchInductor settings:

```yaml
generator:
  engine_init_kwargs:
    compilation_config:
      inductor_compile_config:
        deterministic: true
        batch_invariant: false
        combo_kernels: true
        benchmark_combo_kernel: false
```

`batch_invariant: false` here is TorchInductor's separate reduction-policy
option. vLLM's `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` remained enabled. The native CUDA-graph
capture-size defaults, including size 1, were retained. A separate short-prompt
diagnostic observed ModelRunnerV2 executing full and piecewise graphs, including
full size 1; the full scored runs did not collect per-request graph traces.

The worker installed the published base native wheel, then an editable Python-source candidate with the three IEEE corrections. The release wheel alone does not include those candidate corrections.

The numerical source bindings were:

- Published base native wheel: release
  [`marin-vllm-gpu-20261103-02872a7e5530`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261103-02872a7e5530),
  SHA256 `729cffd23294926b5ddbe1a19485b3da8ad8c582b4ea809ed5350779faa67f83`.
- Candidate `batch_invariant.py`: SHA256
  `2a70d9021f784b27fd409e085093b5bba1e1c0c4a659116bbb7063b647301436`.
- Fixed validation parquet:
  `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/task-selection/snowball-100k/2026.10.23.2/validation.parquet`,
  SHA256
  `958b38bedb04294c6523b21f26cf3aa7a9af43038750bbe849318fbce1a872b7`.

The completed qualification is output version `2026.11.05.2` under
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/dlwh/evals/fixed100-reproducibility/`,
with `job-{1,2}/pass-{0,1}` for the four independently graded passes. Both jobs
finished with task exit 0 and no failures or preemptions. The strict comparison
joined results by frozen canonical task ID, not completion order, with no grade
cache or reuse.

Earlier full-length evaluations on the corrected vLLM candidate with default
compiler policy matched only 91/100 replies across four fresh processes. Two
scores changed in opposite directions while every mean remained 0.20. A later
qualification attempt stopped at 99/100 verified scores after a Daytona snapshot
metadata lookup returned HTTP 502. That failed attempt was preserved. The clean
four-pass qualification above included a bounded retry for read-only snapshot
metadata GET on HTTP 502/503/504; it did not retry grading, creation POSTs, or
failed tasks, or change startup deadlines. The
[lookup retry source change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/8e3f072f01c06b9fe843c3d16ede1bbfc60a54aa)
is tracked in [#11003](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11003).
The qualification used the same retry behavior on Marin
`a2f550d966551876535540063017f85cee01473e`, with `machine.py` SHA256
`42218ba65d5eb62e1ef951197c3e743271928c7b064086848c9e53687c90258a`.
The source PR preserves newer cancellation cleanup on base `3a03f44627bb31916ecea5599fc5fb0a8619458a`; it is a
source port, not a requalification of that newer stack.

These results qualify this finite panel and pinned standalone evaluation
configuration. They do not isolate the cause of the earlier nine reply changes,
prove universal determinism, or qualify training placement and weight transfer
under the concurrent profile. The numerical candidate and lookup retry were
validated on separate source branches. [PR #10760](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10760) retains its
one-sequence recipe and older runtime pin; its exact head has not been run on GPUs. Adopting the
concurrent candidate requires a separate runtime integration and qualification.

## Prior DP4 router measurements

[Xiaoyuan's measurements](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10760#issuecomment-6553179601)
on Snowball v0.1 (Grug-67B-A2B, update 14 from
[#10305](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10305)) attributed most
observed batch variation to the FP32 router. At vLLM `e09cfd55`, its direct
`F.linear` stayed on cuBLAS despite batch-invariant mode. Router logits changed
between batches of one, 2–16, and at least 17 tokens. Moving the router to the
batch-invariant IEEE FP32 kernel improved eager agreement from 23/164 to
161/164 replies with fixed-root expert reduction. Compiled execution reached
162/164 before excluding size-1 CUDA graphs. Both partial results fail an exact
reproducibility check.

On four H100s at DP4, the reported combination produced identical greedy
HumanEval+ replies for all 164 prompts in 13 passes across four launches, at
16 and 64 requests in flight, with different engine placements and request
orders. The report does not specify whether reply equality compared text,
token IDs, or both. The combination was:

- `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` and the router in the batch-invariant IEEE FP32 kernel.
- Fixed-root expert-output reduction: reduce on one rank, then scatter, using
  the reduction change described in vLLM `01911be3`.
- `TORCHINDUCTOR_DETERMINISTIC=1`, Inductor's `benchmark_combo_kernel` disabled,
  and `cudagraph_capture_sizes` excluding 1.

The same report identified a separate long-prompt issue in FlashAttention 3's
sliding-window path: chunk starts needed 32-token alignment to match unsplit
prefill, and concurrent requests could move the split. Chunked prefill disabled
kept long-prompt scoring bit-identical under load; the report gives no panel
size or pass count for that check. The HumanEval+ panel above
also matched with chunked prefill and prefix caching both disabled or both at
vLLM's defaults; that result does not cover every long-prompt chunk boundary.

These measurements used a different checkpoint, panel and DP4 setup.
Xiaoyuan had not tested vLLM `01911be3` as a complete revision, #10760's
`39e62869693c` pin, or DP8/EP8. The IEEE FP32 router result does not qualify
`01911be3`'s TF32 router path. The DP8/EP8 qualification above used a newer
runtime and a different combination:
TRITON attention and native size-1 CUDA graphs remained enabled. It does not
retroactively qualify the older pins or reproduce every setting in Xiaoyuan's
DP4 experiment. Neither finite panel establishes universal bitwise determinism.



## Status

The prefix-cache-off standalone fixed100 qualification is complete. Prefix-cache equivalence is under source investigation; no prefix-on failure has yet been established for the qualified TRITON stack. Runtime adoption and training qualification remain separate.

spillover_issues.title: [experiment] Grug fixed100 serving reproducibility

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

🤖 Scaling-ladder analysis for the **535B-A23B, 18T-token** hero. The ladder trains one uniform hero EP recipe at five widths; four rungs finished and the d2048 rung crashed at ~81%. Fitting a power law across the rungs (`L = 1.5 + A·C^-α`, compute excludes lm_head) and extrapolating to the hero's compute predicts a final **dropless paloma macro-loss ≈ 2.04**.

**Hero prediction by training percentile** — the four measured rungs plus the d6144 hero prediction at every 5% (dashed/hollow = extrapolated).
![hero prediction by percentile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/hero_prediction_by_percentile.png)

**Per-5% scaling-law fits (log-log)** — one power-law fit per training fraction; the crimson points trace the hero prediction out to hero-scale compute, ending at 2.039 @100%.
![scaling law fits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_scaling_laws.png)

**Method check** — a linear extrapolation from each finished rung's 60–80% window predicts its own 100% dropless macro-loss to within ~0.003–0.004 (consistently a hair optimistic, since the curve flattens under cosine decay).
![60-80 extrapolation vs actual](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_extrapolation_60_80.png)

**Full-granularity training cross-entropy** — every step, with the datamix phase-2 boundary at 80% (a small loss bump is visible in every rung at that point).
![training cross-entropy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_train_ce_fullres.png)

Prior precedent for this kind of extrapolation — the 67B-A2B 10T run's preregistered (80%) and two retroactive (21%, 63%) scaling-law fits each predicted that run's target within ~0.6% (issue #6044):
![67B scaling fits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/scaling_fit_67b_prereg_vs_retro.png)

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

And perhaps more importantly, the kernel was a bit buggy if I changed sliding window length. I think it should be good on global layers too, since its limited to just the most recent X (512 or 1024) positions. I am more bullish on relative position embedding + MLA. Since MLA has very janky approach to RoPE, which requires replicating 64 head dims across every head. Relative position embedding fixes this. I think what was happening (guessing) was rare tokens were having their norm driven to near zero, and then getting massive grad when they finally ended up in the batch. comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

comments.author: mindscanlabs
comments.body:
**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

The top-level `macro_loss` instead averages the zeros in ([eval.py#L611](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L611)), about −0.14 on the hero's 23 tags. The 67B's 65K→262K switch, with the same tokenizer and Paloma files, shows both: from step 155,999 ([65K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step141k)) to 156,000 ([262K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k)), `eval/paloma/macro_loss` rose 2.1774 → 2.2150 while the other 14 subsets moved +0.0004, and `eval/macro_loss` fell 2.0260 → 1.8607 (2.0379 without the zeros). Either fix is small: mask zero-token tags in the top-level macro as the group macros already do, or keep all 16 subsets by setting `GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len` (#9890) to 65,536 for the 262K phase.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Weight merging the final hero checkpoints: −0.003 loss at 65K, saved as a resumable checkpoint**

Averaging the final 65K-phase checkpoints lowers loss by about 0.003 on every eval. On the ladder law L = 1.5 + 84.8·C^−0.09 that's worth roughly 7% more training compute, for free.

**Checkpoint:** `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-ctx65k-merge-hb-avg11/checkpoints/step-390251`

- **Weights:** an equal-weight average of 11 checkpoints: 385,500–390,000 every 500 steps, plus the final 390,251. Each weight tensor is rescaled to stay on the hyperball (details below).
- **Training state:** step 390,251, with that checkpoint's full optimizer state and QB betas. It has the hero's checkpoint layout, so it resumes directly with `initialize_from` or loads weights-only for evals and export.
- **`metadata.json`** records the sources, the weights, the merge space and where the training state came from.

All evals are dropless at 65,536 context with `qk_mult` 1.66. Each row is the change versus step 390,000.

| Merge | Clean Paloma | Uncheatable | All evals |
|---|---|---|---|
| step 390,000 (baseline) | 1.7515 | 1.4786 | 1.6953 |
| step 390,251 (final) | −0.0001 | −0.0003 | ±0.0000 |
| average of last 2 | −0.0012 | −0.0011 | −0.0013 |
| average of last 4 | −0.0020 | −0.0020 | −0.0021 |
| EMA, 0.5 per 500 steps (10 ckpts) | −0.0020 | −0.0019 | −0.0021 |
| EMA, 0.8 per 500 steps (10 ckpts) | −0.0028 | −0.0029 | −0.0029 |
| average of 10 (385,500–390,000) | −0.0028 | −0.0031 | −0.0030 |
| average of 10, hyperball | −0.0028 | −0.0031 | −0.0029 |
| **average of 11, hyperball (saved)** | **−0.0030** | **−0.0033** | **−0.0032** |

- **What matters:** how many checkpoints go in, and how evenly they're weighted. The wider and flatter the average, the bigger the gain, and it hadn't levelled off at 11.
- **Hyperball rescaling changes nothing:** the plain average already sits at 0.9995 of the sphere radius.
- **Step-to-step noise is small:** one more stretch of training (390,000 → 390,251) moves the loss by at most 0.0003, an order of magnitude less than the merge.
- **Every eval set improves,** all 23 of them.

**Process**

1. **Choosing eval sets:** the 4K re-evals of the 16K and 65K checkpoints showed which sets don't fall smoothly from step to step. "Clean Paloma" leaves out PTB (contaminated reads), WikiText-103, TwitterAAE and Gab, whose loss rose 7–12 times across those 23 checkpoints. It averages the other 12 sets. "Uncheatable" averages all 7 of its sets.
2. **Merging:** sources load one at a time into a float32 running sum of the fp32 weights. The hero keeps no separate master copy, so these are the master weights.
3. **Hyperball mode:** after averaging, each MuonH/AdamH tensor is rescaled to its sources' mean norm, over the same axes the optimizer holds fixed:
   - 2-D weights: the whole matrix is one ball.
   - Stacked weights: one ball per layer.
   - Routed experts: each layer's whole bank of all 384 experts is one ball (`ALL_EXPERTS`).

   Adam-trained leaves (embeddings, router, norm gains, attention gate) are plain averages.
4. **Saving:** the merged weights are combined with 390,251's step, optimizer state and QB betas, using a template built from the hero's own optimizer config. Before launching, I checked that template against the 390,251 manifest: all 56 optimizer-state arrays and 36 parameter arrays match in shape and dtype.
5. **Verification:** the job reloaded the saved checkpoint and checked the weights bit for bit and the optimizer state by per-leaf checksums. The eval numbers above for the saved row come from that reloaded copy.

Each variant ran as one job on one rack at production priority, logged to W&B in `marin_moe` as `hero-merge-*` (the saved one is `hero-merge-hb-avg11-save`).

**Code:** branch [`larry/hero-ckpt-merge-eval`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/larry/hero-ckpt-merge-eval) at [`dff14a5`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/dff14a54199eaf97a3719d0b6d64a99fb044d47f). The work is in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_checkpoint_eval.py`, using `--merge-source PATH WEIGHT` (repeatable), `--merge-space hyperball` and `--save-merged OUT STATE_FROM`; the CPU tests are in `test_checkpoint_eval.py`. The saved checkpoint was made with:

```
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_checkpoint_eval --run-id hero-merge-hb-avg11-save \
  --merge-source <ckpts>/step-385500 1 ... --merge-source <ckpts>/step-390000 1 --merge-source <ckpts>/step-390251 1 \
  --merge-qk-mult 1.66 --merge-space hyperball \
  --save-merged s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-ctx65k-merge-hb-avg11/checkpoints/step-390251 <ckpts>/step-390251 \
  --seq-len 65536 --version dev --run
```

where `<ckpts>` = `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-ctx65k-step372k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints`.

spillover_issues.body:
`LocalMachineFactory()` fails on some `cw-rno2a` workers with `AttributeError: module 'os' has no attribute 'pidfd_open'`. The task's interpreter on those workers is a uv-cached CPython 3.12.12 (`/uv/cache/python/cpython-3.12.12-linux-x86_64-gnu`), whose `os` module has no `pidfd_open`. Shellbox calls it when it probes bubblewrap (`lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py:572`) and again at `machine.py:386`. Workers of the same job image that resolved CPython 3.12.16 have `os.pidfd_open` and work. `.python-version` pins only `3.12`, so the interpreter depends on what the node has cached.

The error is permanent. A Zephyr pipeline whose workers build a `LocalMachineFactory` fails as a whole: 3 of 4 workers of `/rav/agentic-drafts-ramp-4` hit it on 2026-11-06, and the job failed before any work ran.

```
File "/app/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py", line 1118, in __init__
    self.bwrap = _working_bwrap(_bwrap_candidates(bwrap), system_directories)
File "/app/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py", line 311, in _working_bwrap
    error = _prepare_sandbox(candidate, system_directories)
File "/app/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py", line 572, in _allocate_keeper
    self._keeper_pidfd = os.pidfd_open(self._keeper.pid)
AttributeError: module 'os' has no attribute 'pidfd_open'
```

Reproduce:
1. Submit an Iris job on `cw-rno2a` with `--container-profile container_profile_privileged` whose task runs `python -c "from shellbox.backends.local.machine import LocalMachineFactory; LocalMachineFactory()"`.
2. On a node whose uv cache resolves `3.12` to CPython 3.12.12, the call raises the error above. On a 3.12.16 worker of the same image, `python -c "import os, sys; print(sys.version, hasattr(os, 'pidfd_open'))"` prints `True`; I have not run it on a 3.12.12 worker.

Expected: every worker resolves an interpreter that has `os.pidfd_open`, or `LocalMachineFactory` reports `SandboxUnavailable` with the reason. Passing `-e UV_PYTHON 3.12.16` to the job works around it.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Research**

Iris serializes the submitter's Python as major.minor and passes that to `uv sync --python`, so workers may choose different cached 3.12 patch builds. Shellbox requires `os.pidfd_open` to pin the keeper and init processes, but checks neither that API nor `signal.pidfd_send_signal` before probing bubblewrap. The uv-managed 3.12.13 interpreter in this checkout also lacks both APIs.

Relevant code: [Iris version selection](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L800), [uv setup command](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/setup_scripts.py#L80), [Shellbox keeper](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py#L572), [repository Python pin](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.python-version).

**Proposed Fix**

Pin this repository to the reported working 3.12.16 build, pass the submitter's exact patch version to Iris task setup, and have Shellbox raise `SandboxUnavailable` before starting a probe when its interpreter lacks either required pidfd API. This preserves the pidfd-based process identity and cleanup behavior.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Research**

The factory's bubblewrap probe calls `os.pidfd_open` while starting its keeper ([machine.py:572](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5e8a9cfe9d9d50b79fd03e4ed0ed0087edf627d/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py#L572)); it calls the same API when pinning init ([machine.py:386](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5e8a9cfe9d9d50b79fd03e4ed0ed0087edf627d/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py#L386)). The local uv-managed CPython 3.12.13 lacks both `os.pidfd_open` and `signal.pidfd_send_signal`. Iris generates `uv sync --python 3.12` from the submitter's minor version ([types.py:800](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5e8a9cfe9d9d50b79fd03e4ed0ed0087edf627d/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L800)), so a patch-level `.python-version` pin alone would not determine the task interpreter.

**Proposed Fix**

Pin this checkout to CPython 3.12.15, make Iris's default 3.12 worker setup request at least that patch release, and have `LocalMachineFactory` raise `SandboxUnavailable` with the missing pidfd capability before probing bubblewrap. I installed uv's CPython 3.12.15 locally and confirmed it has both pidfd APIs. This session's uv 0.13.5 catalog does not yet list 3.12.16.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 Fix proposed in #11017: pin Marin to the verified uv CPython 3.12.15 build, make Iris select it for all Python 3.12 task setups, and raise `SandboxUnavailable` when Shellbox lacks a required pidfd API. The nearby Iris and Shellbox tests pass (21 cases); the advisory lint review found no issues. The production-run incident and workaround are recorded in [Echo](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/937).

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 `-e UV_PYTHON 3.12.16` does not work around this. Iris builds the task venv with `uv sync --python 3.12` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py:800` takes only the client's major and minor version), and that flag overrides `UV_PYTHON`. uv prefers managed interpreters, so a node whose `/uv/cache` holds a managed CPython 3.12.12 gets it.

`-e UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE only-system` does work around it. uv then uses the image's own Python, `/usr/local` 3.12.16, which has `os.pidfd_open`. Zephyr child jobs inherit the variable. All 4 workers of `/rav/agentic-drafts-ramp-4c` resolved `/usr/local` 3.12.16, and none raised the error.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Why pods differ.** I compared per-task setup lines and pidfd errors in the `marin` Finelog hub's `log` namespace for `cw-rno2a`, 2026-11-06 03:00–04:00 UTC.

| Run | Worker interpreters selected by uv | Workers logging `AttributeError: module 'os' has no attribute 'pidfd_open'` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `agentic-drafts-ramp-4` | worker 0: 3.12.14; workers 1–3: 3.12.12 | 1–3 |
| `agentic-drafts-ramp-4b` | worker 0: system 3.12.16; workers 1–2: 3.12.14; worker 3: 3.12.12 | 3 |
| `agentic-drafts-ramp-4c` (`UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE=only-system`) | all four: `/usr/local/bin/python3.12` 3.12.16 | none as of 04:35 UTC; job running |

I also inspected live `ramp-4c` pods. Their `/uv/cache` volume is a node-local `hostPath` at `/mnt/local/iris-cache/uv-cache`, so different nodes retain different Python builds. On one live node, the cached 3.12.12 binary lacks both `os.pidfd_open` and `signal.pidfd_send_signal`, while `/usr/local/bin/python` 3.12.16 has both in the same pod and kernel. An isolated `uv python find 3.12` probe chose cached 3.12.12 by default and `/usr/local/bin/python3.12` with `only-system`. A cached 3.12.14 binary on another node has both APIs.

The per-node cache and uv interpreter selection explain the pod-to-pod behavior. The evidence rules out the Linux kernel alone as the cause: two interpreters in one live pod differ in API availability. The exact historical pod images were not retained for comparison.

spillover_issues.author: asartran
spillover_issues.body:
The Harbor unit test `test_run_after_cleanup_starts_a_new_terminal_and_retains_phase_files` fails intermittently in the `harbor-unit` job of the "Marin - Unit" check, which blocks PRs that select that job until someone re-runs it. The test sends `printf first > first.txt` to a tmux-backed terminal, runs agent cleanup, then reads the file, and sometimes the file does not exist yet:

```
FAILED vendor/harbor/tests/unit/agents/terminus_2/test_terminus_2_session_lifecycle.py::test_run_after_cleanup_starts_a_new_terminal_and_retains_phase_files
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/tmp/pytest-of-runner/pytest-0/test_run_after_cleanup_starts_0/guest/workspace/first.txt'
```

It failed in 3 of 12 `harbor-unit` runs observed on Nov 5-6, each time on the assertion at `vendor/harbor/tests/unit/agents/terminus_2/test_terminus_2_session_lifecycle.py:119`, with the other 2,387 tests passing. Re-running the failed job passed both times it was tried. The failures were on branches that do not change Harbor or Shellbox:

- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/42136121653 (#11002)
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/42137901055 (#11004)
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/42165146142 (manual run of #11002's branch)

The test last changed in #10628 on Nov 4.

Reproduce:
1. Run `harbor-unit` (for example by re-running it on any PR that selects it) several times.
2. Some runs fail as above.

Expected: the file written by the first agent run exists by the time `agent.run` and `agent.cleanup` return, so the test passes on every run.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Terminus-2 sends tmux keystrokes and waits for the model's 0.1-second duration, not for shell completion. The lifecycle test marks the task complete immediately afterward; cleanup can close tmux before `printf` creates `first.txt`. [#10735](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10735) edits this test only to add a Linux marker and does not address the timing assumption.

**Relevant code**
- [`tmux_session.py#L716-L733`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/70da6250be4bbc6ed2212ab4f17734883e5a02d3/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/agents/terminus_2/tmux_session.py#L716-L733) — dispatch followed by timed wait
- [`terminus_2.py#L703-L706`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/70da6250be4bbc6ed2212ab4f17734883e5a02d3/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/agents/terminus_2/terminus_2.py#L703-L706) — cleanup closes tmux
- [`test_terminus_2_session_lifecycle.py#L114-L120`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/70da6250be4bbc6ed2212ab4f17734883e5a02d3/vendor/harbor/tests/unit/agents/terminus_2/test_terminus_2_session_lifecycle.py#L114-L120) — assertion assumes command completion

# Proposed Fix

Wait with a bounded deadline for each scripted file write before closing tmux. The test will still verify that cleanup preserves phase files and that a later run starts a new terminal, without relying on 0.1 seconds being enough for CI scheduling.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 [PR #11023](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11023) waits for both scripted writes before terminal cleanup; it closes this issue on merge. The lifecycle test passed 12 consecutive local runs. PR CI passed, including `harbor-unit` and `marin-lint`, and the advisory review found no issues. The local Harbor unit suite had 2,377 passes, one skip, and one backend failure because this Python build lacks `os.pidfd_open`.
